_note: MACHINES, not energy. Complaints/39-machines-are-not-goods.md is the whole brief: a water wheel, a heat engine, a dynamo, a motor and a photovoltaic module are manufactured goods that happen to produce energy, not kinds of energy themselves. Their build bills used to be inlined as `capital` sub-objects inside data/production/70_energy.json's energy-conversion entries, which meant nothing else could buy one, the same machine could not be shared between uses (a water wheel drives a mill, a trip hammer, a bellows AND a dynamo), and a machine could never be improved by one edit that reached every process built on it. Each entry here is an ordinary production recipe like any other in this directory - `inputs`, `labour_hours`, `yield_basis`, `conf` - whose single output is one complete machine, referenced by data/production/70_energy.json's own `capital.build_materials` exactly the way any other capital good in this file is built from real materials rather than a lump of currency (see CAPITAL in _SCHEMA.md). This is a PURE RESHAPE: nothing about what a machine is made of changed, only where that bill of materials lives, so it changes nothing about the price of energy - the same materials and labour go in either way. `requires_node` on each entry copies the gate its energy-consuming entry already carried (they were already labelled); photovoltaic_panel_m2 carries the gate of the silicon its module is built from - see that entry's own yield_basis. None of these entries carries a `capital` of its own: building one machine is a one-off manufacturing job, not a continuously-run process with its own fixed plant to amortise.

waterwheel_unit.basis: per one complete water wheel (undershot or overshot): timber wheel and frame, iron axle and gearing, leat and sluice masonry, ready to run
waterwheel_unit.yield_basis: BUILD BILL, split out of data/production/70_energy.json's mechanical_mj_waterwheel per Complaints/39 (that entry keeps the POWER and LIFE facts that belong to running one, not building one). Timber for the wheel, buckets and frame; iron for the axle, gearing and bearings; stone for the leat and sluice masonry - the same three materials and the same rough order of magnitude as this file's other water-powered plant (iron_bar_kg's finery hearth and hammer; wire_drawn_kg's draw-bench, both in 10_ferrous.json), scaled for a free-standing wheel with its own leat rather than one bolted onto an existing forge. DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED DURING THIS RESHAPE: the axle and gudgeons are bloomery iron (iron_bloom_kg, requires_node mat_wrought_iron), NOT puddled/finery-hearth wrought iron (iron_bar_kg, requires_node finery_puddling, Cort's process, 1784) - a medieval or Roman millwright had no access to Cort's reverberatory hearth at all, and did not need it: bloomery iron, consolidated and hammered, is exactly what a wheel's axle and gearing were historically made of. The old iron_bar_kg figure meant no civilisation before 1784 could build a water wheel in this simulation, despite Domesday recording 5,624 English watermills in 1086 - see Complaints/39. Reported and fixed as a separate step from the pure reshape, exactly as that complaint asks: this single-line change moves the solved price of mechanical_mj and electrical_mj (see the module's own before/after record) because it makes a real technique newly available to England 1300's gated solve, not because any physical quantity here changed - iron_bloom_kg is still 400 kg of iron by mass, just correctly gated iron.

heat_engine_atmospheric_unit.basis: per one complete Newcomen-type atmospheric steam engine: cast/wrought iron cylinder and piston, timber beam, boiler, masonry engine house
heat_engine_atmospheric_unit.yield_basis: BUILD BILL, split out of data/production/70_energy.json's mechanical_mj_heat_engine_atmospheric per Complaints/39 (that entry keeps the POWER and THERMAL-EFFICIENCY facts that belong to running one, not building one). Heavy ironwork for the cylinder, piston and fittings; substantial timber for the rocking beam; a masonry house for the boiler and beam - an engine that was large and crude for its power output, exactly the historical character of the type, which is why it is the FUEL figure on the energy entry, not this build bill, that dominates why this technique never competes with a water wheel.

capital.good: engine works: boring mill, foundry shed and erecting shop
capital.capital_basis: Newcomen engines were built in ironworks with a boring mill for the cylinder, a foundry and an erecting shed; a works of that kind completed a handful of engines in a year. Building and tool masses are order-of-magnitude figures. PASS 9 (Complaint 671): opened en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcomen_atmospheric_engine (hundreds built in the 18th century, over a hundred installed by Newcomen death, cylinders bored at Coalbrookdale and Carron) and the Fairbottom Bobs article (28 in bore, 8 ft stroke, 11 hp, 14 strokes a minute). These bound the engine and the national count (about a hundred in under two decades, several makers), consistent with a handful a year for one works, but no opened page gives the masses of an engine works, so stone, timber and iron stay estimates. PASS 11 (Complaint 671), plant derived from opened buildings. Crew: 5 a year x 650 unit labour hours / 2000 hours a person-year (HOURS_PER_PERSON_YEAR) = 1.62 hands. Floor per hand: the Fort Vancouver Blacksmith's Shop was 45 x 27 ft = 112.9 m2 for eight men, 14.1 m2 a hand, walls about 8 ft (2.44 m) high (National Park Service historic structures report, npshistory.com/publications/fova/hsr/chap5-2.htm); a machine works is denser: Clayton and Shuttleworth, Stamp End Works, Lincoln, 1885 (gracesguide.co.uk/1885_Institution_of_Mechanical_Engineers:_Visits_to_Works): turnery 150 x 110 ft, erecting shop 250 x 90 ft, smiths' shop 150 x 115 ft with 60 forges, iron foundry 13,000 sq ft, over 1700 hands, 6,433 m2 of those four shops / 1700 = 3.8 m2 a hand. At 14.1 m2 a hand the floor is 23 m2 (a 4.8 m square, perimeter 19.1 m); wall volume = perimeter x 2.44 m x 0.45 m (stone walls run 12 to 24 in, midpoint 18 in, dimensions.com/collection/stone-masonry) = 21.0 m3, x 2600 kg/m3 (limestone, Wikipedia Limestone, solid so an upper bound) = 54,660 kg of stone; at 3.8 m2 a hand it is 28,376 kg. Roof framing is 0.041 m3 per m2 of floor (a 42 x 76 ft barn: 3613 board feet of rafters and purlins plus 1500 of sheathing = 5113 x 0.00236 m3 over 296.5 m2, permies.com/t/63545) = 0.94 m3. Build hours: one mason and a helper lay 2.5 cu yd = 1.91 m3 of rubble in a 9-hour day (chestofbooks.com Estimating Part 2), 0.212 m3 an hour, so 99 mason hours and as many helper hours; two men frame 500 board feet of rafters a day (Estimating Part 3), 27.8 board feet a man-hour, so 14 carpenter hours. PASS 12 (Complaint 671), every input now derived from opened sources. Crew: 5 a year x 650 unit hours / 2000 = 1.62 hands. Floor: the geometric mean of 14.1 m2 a hand (Fort Vancouver Blacksmith's Shop, npshistory.com/publications/fova/hsr/chap5-2.htm) and 3.8 m2 a hand (Clayton and Shuttleworth Stamp End works, 1885, gracesguide.co.uk) is 11.9 m2 (assumption: the mean of the two analogues, here 6 to 23 m2), a square 3.4 m on a side, perimeter 13.8 m. Wall height 5.00 m (assumption: the 2.44 m smithy wall for a plain shop; 5 m under a 5-ton hand crane; 9 m under a 20-ton crane). Wall volume = 13.8 m x 5.00 m x 0.45 m (stone walls 12 to 24 in, dimensions.com/collection/stone-masonry) = 31.0 m3, x 2600 kg/m3 (Wikipedia Limestone) = 80704 kg of stone against 80000 in the row (kept, within 3 times). Iron: machine tool masses are from The Fairbanks Company catalogue of 1907 (archive.org illustratedcata00compgoog, full text opened): a lathe of about 11 in swing on a 6 ft bed 1,400 lb, a 24 x 24 in x 5 ft planer 5,300 lb, a 48 x 48 in x 10 ft planer 23,700 lb, its largest lathes 21,500 to 25,000 lb, a drill press about 160 to 170 lb. Crane masses are from Gillette, Handbook of Mechanical and Electrical Cost Data (archive.org handbookofmechan00gill, Table XVIII of Jones's Arizona smelter erection costs): a 5-ton hand traveling crane 3,000 lb and a 20-ton traveling crane 25,200 lb. An anvil is up to 300 lb (Gill, The Blacksmith in Eighteenth-Century Williamsburg, gutenberg.org/ebooks/58318). Tool set (assumption: one tool for each machinist or smith the crew holds, one crane where the parts are heavy): planer 24 in x 24 in x 5 ft 5,300 lb = 2404 kg; lathe 6 ft bed 1,400 lb = 635 kg; anvil 300 lb = 136 kg; 5-ton hand traveling crane 3,000 lb = 1361 kg; total 4536 kg against 4000 in the row (kept, within 3 times). Timber: roof framing 0.041 m3 per m2 of floor (a 42 x 76 ft barn, permies.com/t/63545) x 11.9 m2 = 0.49 m3 plus 2.7 m3 of timber crane gantry (assumption: four 5 m posts and two 5 m beams of 0.3 x 0.3 m section), total 3.2 m3 against 60 in the row; the row is changed. Hours: one mason lays 0.212 m3 of rubble an hour (2.5 cu yd in a 9-hour day, chestofbooks.com Estimating Part 2), so 31.0 m3 / 0.212 = 146 mason hours; framing at 27.8 board feet a man-hour (Estimating Part 3) and 423.8 board feet a m3 is 15.2 hours a m3, so 3.2 m3 = 49 carpenter hours. Fitting: Gillette's Table XVIII gives crane erection labour of $0.65 per 100 lb (read here as labour per 100 lb of machinery, an assumption about the column), and the same book's wage on the Grasselli lead plant foundations was 37.5 cents an hour, so 0.65 / 0.375 = 1.73 hours per 100 lb = 38 hours a tonne; 4.54 t of tools and crane x 38 = 172 fitting hours, split between the trades in the proportion the row had (assumption). Resulting hours: mason 146, carpenter 49, smith 103, millwright 69. Values changed where the derivation differed from the row by more than 3 times. Conf C.

motor_unit.basis: per one complete electric motor: laminated iron core and frame, copper armature and field windings, bearings - the same machine as dynamo_unit above, run in reverse
motor_unit.yield_basis: BUILD BILL, split out of data/production/70_energy.json's mechanical_mj_motor per Complaints/39 (that entry keeps the CONVERSION-EFFICIENCY facts that belong to running one, not building one). A DC motor and a DC dynamo are, to a first approximation, the same physical machine run with the current flowing the other way - a real engineering fact, not a modelling convenience - so this entry's build bill mirrors dynamo_unit's own, slightly lighter since a motor sized to deliver the same shaft power a dynamo there consumed needs a little less copper and iron.

At 14.1 m2 a hand the floor is 38 m2 (a 6.2 m square, perimeter 24.7 m); wall volume = perimeter x 2.44 m x 0.45 m (stone walls run 12 to 24 in, midpoint 18 in, dimensions.com/collection/stone-masonry) = 27.1 m3, x 2600 kg/m3 (limestone, Wikipedia Limestone, solid so an upper bound) = 70,457 kg of stone; at 3.8 m2 a hand it is 36,577 kg. Build hours: one mason and a helper lay 2.5 cu yd = 1.91 m3 of rubble in a 9-hour day (chestofbooks.com Estimating Part 2), 0.212 m3 an hour, so 128 mason hours and as many helper hours; two men frame 500 board feet of rafters a day (Estimating Part 3), 27.8 board feet a man-hour, so 24 carpenter hours. Floor: the geometric mean of 14.1 m2 a hand (Fort Vancouver Blacksmith's Shop, npshistory.com/publications/fova/hsr/chap5-2.htm) and 3.8 m2 a hand (Clayton and Shuttleworth Stamp End works, 1885, gracesguide.co.uk) is 19.8 m2 (assumption: the mean of the two analogues, here 10 to 38 m2), a square 4.4 m on a side, perimeter 17.8 m. Wall height 2.44 m (assumption: the 2.44 m smithy wall for a plain shop; 5 m under a 5-ton hand crane; 9 m under a 20-ton crane). Wall volume = 17.8 m x 2.44 m x 0.45 m (stone walls 12 to 24 in, dimensions.com/collection/stone-masonry) = 19.5 m3, x 2600 kg/m3 (Wikipedia Limestone) = 50765 kg of stone against 8000 in the row (changed). Tool set (assumption: one tool for each machinist or smith the crew holds, one crane where the parts are heavy): lathe 6 ft bed 1,400 lb = 635 kg; drill press 168 lb = 76 kg; total 711 kg against 1200 in the row (kept, within 3 times). Timber: roof framing 0.041 m3 per m2 of floor (a 42 x 76 ft barn, permies.com/t/63545) x 19.8 m2 = 0.81 m3, total 0.8 m3 against 8 in the row; the row is changed. Resulting hours: mason 120, carpenter 12, machinist 15, electrician 12. Values changed where the derivation differed from the row by more than 3 times. Conf C.

Module mass of 10 to 13 kg per m2 and 190 to 250 W per m2 were seen in search summaries (the pv-magazine and epj-pv pages were not opened: 403). No page gave module-line equipment or building masses. PASS 11 (Complaint 671): crew = 15000 m2 x 4.5 unit hours / 2000 = 33.75 hands. Floor at 14.1 m2 a hand (Fort Vancouver Blacksmith's Shop, 45 x 27 ft for eight men, npshistory.com/publications/fova/hsr/chap5-2.htm) is 476 m2, at 3.8 m2 a hand (Clayton and Shuttleworth Stamp End works, 1885, four shops of 6,433 m2 for over 1700 hands, gracesguide.co.uk/1885_Institution_of_Mechanical_Engineers:_Visits_to_Works) 128 m2. A square of 21.8 m side has perimeter 87 m; x 2.44 m x 0.45 m (dimensions.com/collection/stone-masonry, 12 to 24 in) x 2600 kg/m3 = 248 t of stone, and 45 m perimeter at the dense figure gives 128 t, against 46 t in the row (2.8 to 5.4 times); a module line is a clean, taller hall, so the 2.44 m smithy wall is a poor analogue and no value is changed. No opened page gives module-line equipment mass or hall size. PASS 12 (Complaint 671), tried: comparable, the machine-shop tool masses of The Fairbanks Company catalogue of 1907 (archive.org illustratedcata00compgoog, opened: a 6 ft lathe 1,400 lb) with one tool for each of the 11 machinists the 22,500 machinist hours imply (15000 m2 x 1.5 h / 2000, assumption) = 7,000 kg against 4,600 in the row, within 3 times, so the iron is consistent but only as a machine-tool analogue, since wafer saws and diffusion furnaces are not catalogued; rate, Gillette, Handbook of Mechanical and Electrical Cost Data (Table XVIII) erection labour of 38 hours a tonne would give about 270 hours for that 7 t against 4,600 machinist hours in the row, so the fitting hours are not supported by an opened rate for installing process lines; stand-in, the building from the dense Stamp End figure (stone 2.8 times the row) already noted above. photovoltaic_panel_m2.basis: per one square metre of installed photovoltaic module (crystalline-silicon solar panel): tempered-glass cover, aluminium frame, copper wiring and junction box, and the silicon photovoltaic cells themselves
photovoltaic_panel_m2.yield_basis: BUILD BILL, split out of data/production/70_energy.json's electrical_mj_photovoltaic per Complaints/39 (that entry keeps the POWER and SERVICE-LIFE facts that belong to running one square metre, not building it). Glass cover, aluminium frame and copper wiring/junction box are real, modest per-square-metre quantities for a module of this class; the silicon figure (0.5 kg/m2) is a wafer-mass allowance including sawing losses, priced through the silicon_kg entry in 20_nonferrous.json. THE HONEST CAVEAT, carried over unchanged: silicon_kg's own yield_basis is explicit that it omits crystal growth, wafer sawing, cell doping/metallisation and module lamination - real, individually energy-intensive steps in making an actual photovoltaic cell - so this entry's resulting price is a LOWER BOUND by a margin this file cannot yet quantify, not a claim that a panel is already this cheap to build in full. Tag: GAP, not a heuristic, per CLAUDE.md 3.4. requires_node is the node that makes the solar-grade silicon the module is built from (silicon_kg carries the same gate): the tree has no node for the cell itself (nothing marks the step from understanding the photovoltaic effect to manufacturing a cell), and no one can build a module without that silicon, so the silicon's gate is the earliest a module can exist. data/production/70_energy.json's electrical_mj_photovoltaic carries the same gate. The module draws aluminium, which is smelted with electricity, so the cheaper electricity gets the cheaper its own source gets; the solver prices that loop to a fixed point (sim/tests/test_no_seller_no_price.py).

low_voltage_main_two_wire_unit.basis: per one two-wire low-voltage DC main of 800 m route, rated 100 kW at the lamp: copper conductors and the labour that sets its poles
low_voltage_main_two_wire_unit.yield_basis: BUILD BILL of the line plant in electrical_mj_main_two_wire. Current at the lamp is 100 kW over 110 V; the conductor section is that current over the design current density (1500 circular mils per ampere, 1.3157 A per mm2); copper mass is 2 conductors times section times 800 m times 8960 kg/m3. Two conductors, each of the full section. Pole setting: 20 poles (25 per km at a 130 ft span, Still, Overhead Electric Power Transmission, 1913, pp. 40-41) at 45 a day (40 to 50 a day by two linemen and a teamster, Standard Handbook Sec. 11 par. 167) is 0.444 crew-days of two linemen (electrician) and one teamster (labourer) at 8 hours a day (the day length is an assumption). LOWER BOUND ON THE PLANT: the conductor copper and the pole-setting labour are counted; the pole timber, crossarms, insulators and stringing labour are not, because no mass or hours table for them was read (the electricity market design report marks them needed). Meter, meter reading and station attendant hours are likewise not counted.

capital.good: installer's wagon, cable drum gear and tools
capital.capital_basis: A cable crew lays a main with a horse wagon, drum gear and hand tools; the entry states eleven hours of crew time a main and a crew works about fifteen hundred hours a year, so about a hundred and forty mains. Masses are reasoned estimates. PASS 11 (Complaint 671), every figure from a page opened in that pass. Horse: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percheron gives draft horses of 860 kg (American average) and 910 to 1,000 kg (British stallions), so 1000 kg of draught animal is at the top of that range. Wagon timber and iron: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density gives oak at 710 kg per m3, so 3 m3 is about 2.1 t of timber; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wain gives a Western freight wagon (16 ft body, 7 ft rear wheels) at 7,800 lb (3,500 kg) empty, so a lighter cable wagon of about 2.3 t (timber plus 200 kg of iron) is within a factor of 2 of it; cottagecraftworks.com 'Farm Wagon Gear, Steel Spoke-Rim Wheels' (a modern vendor page) lists running gear for a six-ton wagon at 600 lb (272 kg), the same order as the 200 kg of tyres, axles and drum gear here. Build hours: a school folklore record (duchas.ie, Knockanevin school, https://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes/4921831/4910262/5183994) says 'A carpenter takes three days to make a pair of wheels' (two pairs, so about 48 hours at 8 hours a day), and National Geographic (https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/master-ox-cart-maker-keeps-ancient-craft-rolling-motorized-world) says an ox-cart maker 'spends a month assembling each cart', so 80 carpenter plus 60 smith hours (140 in all) is the same order as one cart. Service life: hobbyfarms.com (https://www.hobbyfarms.com/red-wagon-farm-equipment/, a hobbyist account) describes a farm wagon 'maybe not 20 years old, but close to it' with one wooden side rebuilt, so 10 years is half of that. Annual output: crew time a main is this entry's 7.11 electrician plus 3.56 labourer hours, 10.67 hours; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_time (OECD table) gives 1,332 to 2,226 hours a year per worker, so 1,500 hours / 10.67 = 140 mains a year. Sources are modern, vendor, folklore and hobbyist pages (weak), but each number has an opened page of the same order.
